en: In the *Buddhamātṛ-sūtra*, at that time, when the World-Honored One had entered parinirvāṇa, he lay propped up and addressed the great assembly, saying:
"I now desire to enter parinirvāṇa; I have not seen Ānanda and my Kāśyapa. When they come, tell them these words: 'I..."
"I shall not see you again.
He then dispatched Upāli to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to inform my mother:
"My entire body is in inconceivable pain; I pray that you come soon to pay homage to the Triple Gem."
At that time, during the middle watch of the night, the Mother of the Buddha had six kinds of ominous dreams:
first, she dreamed that a mountain of precious jewels collapsed;
second, she dreamed that the four oceans dried up.
Third, he dreamed that frost fell in the fifth month;
fourth, he dreamed that jeweled banners and streamers were broken and severed, and that canopies and flowers collapsed;
fifth, he dreamed that four fires came to burn his body.
Sixth, she dreamed that her two breasts spontaneously flowed with milk.
At that time, before the Buddha’s mother had finished recounting her dreams, Upāli was seen coming through the air.
He asked: "From what direction has the Sage come?
Your countenance is haggard and your face lacks luster; you appear like a timid person."
Then Upāli, with a choked and hoarse voice, remained silent for a long time.
He then said:
"O Mother of the Buddha!"
O Mother of Buddhas!
Our Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, last night at the hour of midnight, relinquished his great Dharma-body and entered parinirvāṇa.
He has therefore sent me here to request that you assemble the assembly of kinsmen.

At that time, having heard these words, the Buddha’s mother covered her face with her hands; she appeared as if Mount Sumeru had collapsed, her entire body manifesting like a palāśa flower, and she fell to the ground in a swoon.
At that time, two goddesses sprinkled him with water, and after a long while, he regained consciousness.
Then, the Mother of the Buddha, accompanied by her retinue and surrounded by them in reverence, descended from Mount Sumeru to the space between the twin śāla trees.
When the Tathāgata Samyagdarśin had completed his enshrinement and funeral rites, there remained only his saṃghāṭī robe, folded and placed by the side of the coffin;
his alms bowl and mendicant’s staff were hung upon a tree.
Two lions died by cutting their own throats;
the ten great disciples wailed toward the heavens.
At that time, the Buddha’s mother, holding these objects in her hands, spoke these words:
"This is my son; while he was alive, he used these items to transform and guide sentient beings.
These items now have no master!
At that time, the Buddha’s mother circumambulated the coffin three times, then stood to one side and, weeping in distress, spoke, saying:
“O Compassionate Son! You are my son, and I am your mother.
Now that you are entering parinirvāṇa, why do you not leave behind even half a verse of the Dharma?”

At that time, hearing his mother’s call, the Tathāgata caused the golden coffin to open of its own accord. He sat back upon a pedestal of a thousand-petaled lotus flower and preached the Dharma for his mother:
“The world is suffering and empty; all conditioned phenomena are impermanent. These are the laws of arising and ceasing;
when arising and ceasing have ceased, nirvāṇa is bliss.”
At that time, the Mother of the Buddha, having heard this Dharma, felt joy arise in her heart and returned to her original heaven.
Before she had reached the celestial abode, she stood poised in mid-air; with a heart of compassion, she cried out "Alas! and wept bitterly.
Heaven and earth shook, and tears fell like rain.
The hundred birds in the clouds all uttered cries of lamentation.
All things born of affection must eventually part; how can it be that the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa?
The Buddha of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra.
